Why is Disney eating the scraps of bankrupt Character.AI?

Fact check passed on this exact text: eight sentences signed off by Krish on 28 October 2026Prediction kept as recorded (1 March 2027, 75%)Both cuts watched in full and approved by Krish on 28 October 2026

The idea, the story's flow, the ending, the takeaway, the angle and the tone, agreed before the drafts are written.

Record-ready briefAgreed 26 Oct
The idea
Why did Google and Disney both pay for Character.AI, and what does it mean for any business that runs on someone else's AI?
The story, beat by beat
  1. Google paid for the brains: a reported $2.7 billion in 2024 for the tech, and it hired the founders.
  2. Disney tried renting first: a $1 billion deal to put 200+ characters in OpenAI's Sora, which OpenAI shut in March.
  3. Now Disney is buying the team: 66 staff at about $60 million a year, and a $20 million opening bid for the code, through a bankruptcy it required.
  4. Who is left with the shell: the users and the lawsuits stay with Character.AI.
  5. Our prediction: by 1 March 2027, Skydance, Universal Music Group and Comcast's NBCUniversal each announce buying an AI company or its team (75%).
The ending
Here's what I'd do with this info if I were you: ask four things about the firm behind your main AI tool. Founders still there? Main product or side bet? Short of cash? Collecting lawsuits?
The takeaway
The money followed the people, and everyone else was left with the empty box. Watch your AI supplier for the warning signs years before the end.
The angle
follow.the.money: two giants, two receipts, one empty box.
The tone
Observational and witty, dry on true details (Disney 'respected the decision').
Who it is for
A leader whose business leans on AI tools made by someone else.

The article and the scripts. Edit any paragraph or comment on any passage; your saves and comments shape the next version.

The words are signed off. The article is under Publish, in its first step; the scripts are under Record.

Video script (5-minute cut)
Disney asked a dying AI firm to go bust first. That way it could hire the team and leave the lawsuits behind. So why are Disney and Google both paying for pieces of the same company? And what does it mean for you?

I've been reading the court papers on Character.AI, the app where millions of people chat with made-up characters. Two giants have now paid for pieces of it, for very different reasons. So I wanted to break it down for you.

Let's start with Google. Google wanted the brains behind the app. So in 2024, it reportedly paid two point seven billion dollars to use Character.AI's tech. And it hired the founders and their research team away. Google was racing to build the smartest AI, and these people were very good at it. But the rest of the staff stayed behind, and the app carried on, until its cash started running low.

Now, Disney wanted something else, and to see why, go back to last December. Disney agreed to put a billion dollars into OpenAI. As part of that deal, over two hundred Disney characters would star in Sora, OpenAI's video app. But Sora belonged to OpenAI. So Disney was really renting space for Mickey, Marvel and Star Wars on someone else's app.

Then in March, OpenAI shut Sora down. The deal died, and no money changed hands. Disney said it respected the decision, which is a very polite way to say, well, that's awkward.

So Disney changed its plan. In September, it hired Character.AI's chief executive, who ran the firm after the founders left. He got a brand new job, Disney's first ever technology chief. And this month, the court papers show the rest of the plan. Disney has offered jobs to sixty-six of Character.AI's staff. All together, their pay comes to about sixty million dollars a year, for three years. On top of that, Disney has bid twenty million dollars for the code. That includes its tools for keeping children safe.

Here's the clever bit. Character.AI filed for bankruptcy on the twelfth of October. And Disney made that a condition of its offer, and the papers even say why. Character.AI was running low on cash. And it faced lawsuits from families and US states, who say its chatbots harmed children. Going through the court means Disney takes the people and the code, clean, while the lawsuits stay behind with Character.AI.

So who is left holding the empty box? The people who used the app, for a start. Disney didn't bid for the app itself, or for anyone's chats. So what happens to the app is now up to the court. And then there are the people suing Character.AI, whose claims stay with a firm that is being sold for parts.

See, the money followed the people. Google paid billions for the tech and the founders, and Disney is paying millions for the rest of the team. Everyone else is left with the empty box.

And it isn't just Disney. Netflix bought an AI film start-up this year, and the record label Warner Music bought an AI firm too. The big media firms have stopped renting AI, and started owning it.

So my prediction is that three more giants follow them. First, Skydance, the new owner of Paramount Pictures. Then the record label Universal Music. And then Comcast, the American TV giant that owns NBC. By the first of March, 2027, I reckon each of them will announce buying an AI firm or its team. And I'm seventy-five percent sure all three will do it.

Now, why should you care if you're not Disney? Because most businesses now run on someone else's AI. It might be your writing tool, your chatbot, or maybe your whole customer service desk. If that supplier goes the way of Sora, the tool can switch off. And your work in it can go too. And this story shows the warning signs, years before the end.

Here's what I'd do with this info if I were you. Pick the AI tool your business leans on most, and ask four things about the firm that makes it. First, are its founders still there? Google took Character.AI's founders two years before the end. Second, is your tool the main thing that firm sells, or a side bet? Sora was a side bet, and it vanished. Third, is the firm running short of cash? The court papers warned about exactly that. And fourth, is it collecting lawsuits? That's why Disney went through the court. If two of those answers worry you, line up a plan B now. That means a second tool you've tried on real work, and a copy of your own data.

The full deep dive is at makeyourmindup.ai.
Video script (90-second cut)
I've been reading court papers on Character.AI, a chat app with millions of users. It ran low on cash, faced lawsuits over harm to children, and went bust. So why did Google, and now Disney, both pay for it?

Google got the brains first. In 2024 it reportedly paid two point seven billion dollars to use the tech, and hired the founders away.

Disney wanted its characters in AI videos, so it agreed a billion-dollar deal with OpenAI's video app, Sora. Then OpenAI shut Sora down.

So Disney is building its own team, hiring sixty-six staff on sixty million dollars a year in total. And by buying through the bankruptcy court, Disney leaves the lawsuits behind.

So my prediction? I reckon that by March 2027, Skydance, Universal Music and Comcast each buy an AI team too. I'm seventy-five percent sure all three will.

Here's what I'd do with this info if I were you. Ask four things about the firm behind your AI. Are its founders still there? Is your tool its main product? Is it short of cash? And is it piling up lawsuits?

Title
Why is Disney eating the scraps of bankrupt Character.AI?
Subtitle
Why did Google and Disney both pay for Character.AI, and what does it mean for any business that runs on someone else's AI?
The article, with its pictures in place

Disney asked a dying AI company to go bust first, so it could hire the team and leave the lawsuits behind.

That company is Character.AI, the app where millions of people chat with made-up characters. It filed for bankruptcy in Delaware on 12 October. Google and Disney have now paid for pieces of it, two years apart, for two very different reasons. And the people who used it are left holding whatever remains.

One question, then. Why did Google and Disney both pay for Character.AI, and what does it mean for any business that runs on someone else's AI?

GOOGLE PAID FOR THE BRAINS

In August 2024, Google reportedly paid $2.7 billion to license Character.AI's technology. A spokesperson told Wired that the licence covered the technology as it stood at the time, and that Google also hired the founders and other members of their research team.

The "vast majority" of the staff stayed at Character.AI, the same spokesperson said. The app kept running too, as if nothing much had happened.

My read on Google is simple: it wanted the people who built Character.AI, and a licence to use what they had built. So it paid for both, and left the company standing.

Keep that date in your head. August 2024 is when the founders went to Google. The bankruptcy came in October 2026. That's the first warning sign in this story, and it was easy to miss.

DISNEY TRIED RENTING FIRST

Disney's reason starts somewhere else entirely.

In December 2025, Disney agreed to put $1 billion into OpenAI and to let more than 200 of its characters appear in Sora, OpenAI's video app. Marvel, Pixar and Star Wars would all be in there. A big bet, with one catch: every one of those characters would live on someone else's app.

Then in March 2026, OpenAI said it would shut its Sora app. The Disney deal went with it, and reports say no money had changed hands. Disney said it respected the decision, which is the corporate way of saying it had just been left standing in the rain.

My read is that the rest of the story turns on this moment. Disney had licensed its characters to someone else's app, and that app closed.

NOW DISNEY IS BUYING THE TEAM

So Disney changed its approach. In September it hired Character.AI's chief executive as its first chief technology officer. Then came the court papers.

Disney has offered jobs to 66 of Character.AI's staff, most of the workforce. Their pay comes to about $60 million a year for three years, around $180 million in all, according to the filings reported by Gizmodo. On top of that, Disney has made the opening $20 million bid for rights to Character.AI's technology, a bid other buyers can still beat. Wired reports that the list covers its code, its trust and safety tools, its training infrastructure and its age-prediction technology.

Here is the part I keep coming back to. The filings say Disney required the deal to go through the bankruptcy court, because of Character.AI's "diminishing cash reserve and significant litigation and regulatory risks". Wired reports that a draft court order would leave Character.AI responsible for "any liability or other obligation" it might have.

If the court approves, Disney gets the people and much of the code. Character.AI keeps the legal fights.

Clever or cold? Probably both.

Why Character.AI, of all the AI companies Disney could have chosen?

Look at what each side owns. Disney owns Marvel, Pixar and Star Wars, and Character.AI's app lets millions of people chat with made-up characters. After Sora, Disney seems to have decided it would rather own the team that does this than rent space on someone else's app. The fit is almost too neat. That's my inference from the timing and the filings; Disney hasn't said it in those words.

WHO IS LEFT WITH THE SHELL

Two groups stay behind.

First, the people who used the app. According to Wired, the list of what Disney is bidding for leaves out users' data and Character.AI's website, and the court filing leaves out its consumer-facing apps. What happens to the app now is up to the court. (If I'd spent two years chatting to a made-up character on there, I'd want to know where those chats end up.)

Second, everyone with a claim against it. Families sued Character.AI, saying its chatbots harmed children; those families agreed to settle, and a referee approved each settlement on 11 October, the day before the bankruptcy. When it filed, 46 states and territories were investigating it, and several states have sued. Wired reports the deal is built so that whatever is left of Character.AI keeps responsibility for those legal battles, some of them still going.

So the money followed the people. Google paid $2.7 billion to use the tech and hire the founders. Disney is paying millions for the rest of the team. Everyone else gets the empty box.

If your business runs on someone else's AI, this is the part worth sitting with. You can't stop your supplier being bought or shut down. You can spot the signs early, and in this story they showed up years before the end.

OUR PREDICTION

So what does it mean beyond Disney? My read: the companies with the most to lose are deciding that renting their AI is too risky.

Disney isn't alone. This year Netflix bought InterPositive, an AI filmmaking start-up, in a deal reported at $587 million. Warner Music bought Sureel AI in June. WildBrain, the company behind the Teletubbies, bought Personality AI in August. (Yes, the Teletubbies' owner now has an AI company.)

Put those together and a pattern shows. The big media companies are moving from renting AI to owning it.

Three of the biggest haven't made that move yet. Skydance, which now owns Paramount and Warner Bros after its merger closed on 6 October, calls the combined company "tech-forward". Universal Music has struck agreements with AI companies, including Nvidia, but we could find none it has bought, while its rival Warner Music has. NBCUniversal has made no AI purchase that we could find.

Each of them now has a rival that has bought, and Disney has just shown everyone what renting can cost. That's why I think they move next.

Our prediction. By 1 March 2027, Skydance, Universal Music Group and Comcast's NBCUniversal will each have announced buying an AI company or its team. How sure we are: 75%.

Why not higher? All three have to move inside about four months, and any one of them could decide that renting is fine for now.

If the giants with the deepest pockets won't leave their AI in someone else's hands, it's worth knowing whose hands yours is in.

3 things you can do tomorrow

1. Write down the AI tools your business would struggle without, and who makes each one. Most leaders know the tools. Fewer know whether the maker is a giant, a start-up or a giant's side project. 2. For the one you lean on most, answer four questions about its maker. Are its founders still there? Is your tool its main product or a side bet? Is it short of cash? Is it collecting lawsuits? Google hired Character.AI's founders in August 2024, two years before the bankruptcy; OpenAI shut its Sora video app; and the court filing warned about cash and litigation. 3. If two of those answers worry you, pick your plan B now. Choose the tool you would move to, and try it on one real task this month, while you still have time to switch calmly.

Copy
Post text
Character.AI filed for bankruptcy on 12 October. In 2024 Google paid $2.7 billion for a licence to its technology and to hire its founders. Disney is now offering jobs to 66 of its staff at about $60 million a year, with a $20 million opening bid for the code, and the lawsuits stay behind.

So the money followed the people, and everyone else got the empty box.

If your business runs on someone else's AI, the full piece has four questions to ask your supplier: are its founders still there, is this its main product, is it short of cash, and is it piling up lawsuits.

Episode title
Why is Disney eating the scraps of bankrupt Character.AI?
Description
Disney has asked a dying AI company to go bust, so it can hire the team and leave the lawsuits behind. Google paid $2.7 billion for the same company's founders two years ago. I read the court papers on Character.AI to work out why both giants paid for a piece of it, who is left holding the empty box, and what it means if your business runs on someone else's AI.
